final.title: When definitions drift, start with one workflow
final.body:
If your team keeps using the same word three different ways, treat that as a workflow problem first. The useful question is not “is the business broken?” It is: which single recurring workflow shows signs that the same field, label, or category is being read differently each time?

Start there. Pick one process only: invoices, customer records, handoffs, or email triage. Then count the drift for two weeks. Track every time someone has to recategorise something, ask for clarification, fix a duplicate record, or redo an approval because the definition was unclear. Count actual instances, not impressions. That gives you a real threshold for deciding whether the issue is just messy paperwork or a rule that needs tightening.

If the workflow depends on human judgment, policy sign-off, or context outside the written rule, AI is a helper, not a replacement. A grounded knowledge assistant can check approved definitions in company documents before it answers, but that is still support, not authority. For money movement and other high-risk decisions, the owner still approves it.

If you want, the next practical step is to write down the one workflow and the one definition that keeps drifting, then see where the rework lands. The tea leaves are usually in the admin stack, not the air.

final.title: Start with the one workflow where definitions blur
final.body:
If your team uses the same word three different ways, that is usually a workflow problem before it is a systems problem. The useful question is: which single recurring process shows the drift first? It might be invoices, customer records, handoffs, or email triage. Pick one workflow and leave the rest alone for now. Small businesses do not need a grand cleanup plan; they need the next clear decision.

Then count the rework. For two weeks, track each time someone has to recategorise a record, ask for clarification, fix a duplicate, or rework an approval because the definition was unclear. Count actual instances. Do not estimate. If the number is too fuzzy to count, that is already a signal.

Once you can see the pattern, test whether a grounded assistant would help. In plain terms, that means software that checks approved definitions in company documents before it answers or routes work. If the task needs human judgment, policy sign-off, or context outside the written rule, AI stays a helper. And for money movement or other high-risk decisions, the owner still approves it.

If you use customer-owned accounts and hand over finished code, keep that as policy, not a promise of magic. Definitions drift quietly; the fix should not.
